URL: https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611269924
Iran International, 26 November 2026

The Behjatabad facility stands out among similar underground complexes built across Iran for its unusually rapid pace of construction, according to the institute, which published satellite imagery provided by Vantor Technologies.

The complex lies midway between the Isfahan nuclear site and Pickaxe Mountain near Natanz, approximately 62 kilometers from each. Its outer security perimeter is expected to encompass roughly 12,000 acres (5,000 hectares).

The site's security measures, the nature and pace of construction and Iran’s previous construction practices suggest the complex could serve several military purposes, including housing missile systems or other major weapons systems, the institute said.

“A nuclear purpose cannot be ruled out,” it added.

The facility was first identified by satellite imagery analyst Ben Tzion Macales, who said in a November 17 post on X that construction activity had accelerated following Operation Epic Fury, the US military campaign against Iran earlier this year.

The scale of construction activity was such that progress could be tracked even using relatively low-resolution Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, Macales added.

Satellite imagery reviewed by Vantor showed that initial construction activity began in December 2025 and expanded considerably throughout 2026.

The institute said it would publish additional satellite imagery and a more detailed assessment of the facility in a forthcoming report.

Construction of the Behjatabad complex comes as the Islamic Republic has sought to rebuild and reinforce some of its underground facilities following attacks on its nuclear and military infrastructure during the 12-day and 40-day wars.

An assessment published by the institute on November 21, 2025, five months after the 12-day war, found that the June attacks on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan had inflicted extensive and, in some cases, catastrophic damage on Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.

Iran was unable at the time to enrich uranium on a significant scale or manufacture large numbers of centrifuges and had made little progress in restoring its damaged capabilities, according to the assessment.

Researchers warned, however, that the destruction of Iran’s main enrichment facilities did not mean all of its sensitive nuclear capabilities had been eliminated.

Satellite imagery at the time showed activity consistent with debris removal, equipment recovery and efforts to reinforce some facilities.

Among the facilities examined by the institute was Pickaxe Mountain, an underground complex near Natanz that was not targeted during the 12-day war in June 2025.

Iran announced in 2020 that it intended to establish a facility capable of assembling thousands of centrifuges annually at the complex.

Construction of the new facility was approaching completion by November 2025, according to the institute’s assessment.

Researchers identified Pickaxe Mountain as one of the potential sites where Iran could restore parts of its centrifuge manufacturing and assembly capabilities or potentially resume uranium enrichment.

The institute also examined reconstruction at Taleghan 2, a facility within the Parchin military complex that was targeted by Israel in October 2024.

100%Satellite imagery shows the tunnel complex under construction at Iran’s Behjatabad underground facility on November 24, 2026. (Vantor Technologies/Institute for Science and International Security)$RS("S:1a","P:1a")At least three sites associated with possible weapons-related activities had undergone clearance work following attacks, the institute said in its November 2025 assessment.

The whereabouts and condition of Iran’s stockpile of some 440 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% remain among the major unresolved questions surrounding its nuclear program.

Restrictions on access to Iranian nuclear facilities had prevented the International Atomic Energy Agency from fully accounting for the stockpile, the institute said in its November 2025 assessment.

The agency assessed at the time that the material had probably not been removed from the main nuclear sites at Isfahan, Fordow and Natanz, although it could have been relocated within those complexes.

Satellite imagery alone cannot establish what activities are taking place inside Iran’s underground facilities, where its enriched uranium is stored or the condition of its nuclear equipment, according to the institute.

The rapid construction at Behjatabad adds to the growing importance of underground facilities in assessing the future of Iran’s nuclear and military programs.

"])•••$RC("B:5","S:5")More StoriesIranian truckers’ strike spreads to more cities on fifth day, union saysNov 26, 2026, 09:33 GMT+0Listen to this article100%Trucks line in Isfahan, central Iran, during a strike on November 25, 2026.Iranian truck drivers entered a fifth day of strikes on Thursday, with their union saying drivers in 18 cities were refusing to haul freight at rates that have stayed flat as the cost of keeping a truck on the road has climbed.

The Union of Truck Drivers and Trucking Associations Across Iran named Isfahan, Kermanshah in the west and Kazerun in the southern province of Fars among the cities in a message to drivers on Telegram. Truckers in Shiraz stopped work on Sunday, the day the strike began.

The union urged drivers to hold out for higher rates, saying that when one driver agreed to carry a load for next to nothing, others lost out too.

"Tires are priced in dollars, oil is priced in dollars, diesel is priced in dollars," the union said. "So freight rates have to reflect reality too." The rial fell past 2.8 million to the dollar on the open market this week, a record low.

Drivers also face higher insurance premiums, tolls and repair bills, according to the union. "Until we get what we're owed, we won't haul freight," it said.

Diesel shortages, limited supplies of engine oil and tires, and the rising cost of maintaining an aging fleet threatened freight transport across Iran, the union said in a separate statement.

Factories rely on the same trucks to move their goods as farmers do to get crops to market, it said. If those problems persist, production, distribution and prices would all be affected. Farmers had voiced support for the drivers on Wednesday, the union said.

Most of Iran's goods move by road, so truckers' strikes can quickly be felt in shops and markets. In 2018, a truckers' strike over pay and costs spread to hundreds of cities, and the judiciary threatened strikers with harsh punishment.

Listen to this article100%Syrian forces have seized weapons smuggled from Iran's Revolutionary Guards that were bound for Lebanon, US Central Command said on Wednesday, the latest in a string of seizures as Damascus and Beirut move to choke off the routes that once kept Hezbollah armed.

Syria's interior ministry announced two seizures of weapons bound for Lebanon in the countryside around Damascus, on November 20 and 22, and arrested one suspect.

On November 22, the Lebanese army said it had seized 264 kilograms of explosives, including about 203 kilograms of C4, smuggled from Syria, and arrested three people.

Syria's drug enforcement department also seized what CENTCOM called "enormous quantities" of Captagon pills at the border with Lebanon this month.

"Syrian Internal Security Forces confiscated weapons smuggled from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that were bound for Lebanon," Admiral Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, said in a statement.

"These efforts support a stable, unified, and peaceful Syria and reinforce regional security and stability."

For decades, Syria was Iran's main route to Hezbollah. Weapons moved from Iran through Iraq, crossing into Syria at Al-Bukamal on the Iraqi border, and on to Lebanon's Bekaa Valley through official and unofficial crossings, with the help of Bashar al-Assad's government and its security forces.

Revolutionary Guards forces and Iran-backed militias were based across the country.

The fall of Assad in December 2024 cut that route. Syria's new government, many of whose leaders fought against Assad, Hezbollah and the Guards during the civil war, has made a point of intercepting arms bound for the group and naming it in its announcements.

The smuggling has adapted rather than stopped. In July, Syrian authorities seized advanced weapons bound for Hezbollah hidden in a tanker traveling from Iraq.

Much of what is now intercepted on the way to Lebanon is believed to be weapons Hezbollah stockpiled in Syria during the Assad years.

Under Assad, Syria became the world's largest producer of Captagon, an amphetamine-type pill smuggled across the Middle East, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year that Western governments said was run with the involvement of senior figures in his government.

The new authorities have made seizures a public priority, and Washington has rewarded the shift: the United States lifted most of its sanctions on Syria in 2025, and in August removed it from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
